claim: CLC-2 is a voltage-gated chloride channel that contributes to electrical excitability and ion homeostasis in many different tissues.
source: CLC-2 is a voltage-gated chloride channel that contributes to electrical excitability and ion homeostasis in many different tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement about CLC-2 function, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Among the nine mammalian CLC homologs, CLC-2 is uniquely activated by hyperpolarization, rather than depolarization, of the plasma membrane.
source: Among the nine mammalian CLC homologs, CLC-2 is uniquely activated by hyperpolarization, rather than depolarization, of the plasma membrane.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about CLC-2 voltage dependence and comparison to other CLC homologs.

claim: CryoEM structures of human CLC-2 were determined at 2.46 – 2.76 Å resolution.
source: Here, we report cryoEM structures of human CLC-2 at 2.46 – 2.76 Å, in the presence and absence of the selective inhibitor AK-42.
evidence: The resolution values are directly reported from the experimental data obtained in this study.

claim: AK-42 binds within the extracellular entryway of the Cl–-permeation pathway.
source: AK-42 binds within the extracellular entryway of the Cl–-permeation pathway, occupying a pocket previously proposed through computational docking studies.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing AK-42 density in the cryoEM map at this location.

claim: AK-42 occupies a pocket previously proposed through computational docking studies.
source: AK-42 binds within the extracellular entryway of the Cl–-permeation pathway, occupying a pocket previously proposed through computational docking studies.
evidence: This refers to prior computational work that predicted the binding site, now confirmed by structural data.

claim: In the apo structure, two distinct conformations involving rotation of one of the cytoplasmic C-terminal domains (CTDs) were observed.
source: In the apo structure, we observed two distinct conformations involving rotation of one of the cytoplasmic C-terminal domains (CTDs).
evidence: This is directly observed in the structural data from 3D classification.

claim: An intracellular N-terminal 15-residue hairpin peptide nestles against the TM domain to physically occlude the Cl–-permeation pathway.
source: In the absence of CTD rotation, an intracellular N-terminal 15-residue hairpin peptide nestles against the TM domain to physically occlude the Cl–-permeation pathway.
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map showing the hairpin structure blocking the pore.

claim: The N-terminal hairpin peptide is highly conserved among species variants of CLC-2 but is not present in other CLC homologs.
source: This peptide is highly conserved among species variants of CLC-2 but is not present in other CLC homologs.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal hairpin of CLC-2 stabilizes a closed state of the channel by blocking the cytoplasmic Cl–-permeation pathway.
source: Through electrophysiological studies of an N-terminal deletion mutant lacking the 15-residue hairpin peptide, we support a model in which the N-terminal hairpin of CLC-2 stabilizes a closed state of the channel by blocking the cytoplasmic Cl–-permeation pathway.
evidence: This is supported by both structural data showing the hairpin blocking the pore and electrophysiological data from the deletion mutant.

claim: The CLC 'Chloride Channel' family encompasses both electrodiffusive chloride (Cl−) channels and secondary active transporters that stoichiometrically exchange Cl− for protons (H+).
source: The CLC 'Chloride Channel' family encompasses both major ion-transport mechanisms: half of the CLC homologs are electrodiffusive chloride (Cl−) channels, and half are secondary active transporters that stoichiometrically exchange Cl− for protons (H+) (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CLC family, supported by citation.

claim: CLC channels are 'broken' transporters.
source: The occurrence of two mechanisms in one family suggests they operate by variations on a common theme (Miller, 2006), and experimental results revealed that CLC channels are 'broken' transporters (Lísal and Maduke, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited experimental work.

claim: A conserved glutamate residue referred to as the 'gating glutamate' (Egate) plays a central mechanistic role in both CLC channels and transporters.
source: In both CLC channels and transporters, a conserved glutamate residue referred to as the 'gating glutamate' (Egate) plays a central mechanistic role.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CLC proteins supported by extensive literature.

claim: High-resolution CLC transporter structures show that the Egate residue can adopt four different conformations.
source: High-resolution CLC transporter structures show that this residue can adopt four different conformations (Dutzler et al., 2002; Dutzler et al., 2003; Feng et al., 2010; Chavan et al., 2020; Schrecker et al., 2020, Figure 1A), which contribute to the Cl−/H+ exchange mechanism (Accardi and Miller, 2004; Feng et al., 2012; Chavan et al., 2020; Leisle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited structural studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The four Egate conformations contribute to the Cl−/H+ exchange mechanism in CLC transporters.
source: High-resolution CLC transporter structures show that this residue can adopt four different conformations (Dutzler et al., 2002; Dutzler et al., 2003; Feng et al., 2010; Chavan et al., 2020; Schrecker et al., 2020, Figure 1A), which contribute to the Cl−/H+ exchange mechanism (Accardi and Miller, 2004; Feng et al., 2012; Chavan et al., 2020; Leisle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional and structural studies.

claim: CLC-K is the lone CLC homolog lacking the Egate.
source: The first CLC channel structure reported was of bovine CLC-K (Park et al., 2017), a kidney-expressed homolog that is the lone CLC homolog lacking the Egate (Kieferle et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature on CLC-K structure and sequence.

claim: One cryoEM structure of human CLC-1 shows Egate in the 'out' position.
source: The only other CLC channel structures reported prior to 2023 are of the human CLC-1: one of these cryoEM structures shows Egate in the 'out' position (Park and MacKinnon, 2018) while the other lacked density for Egate (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited CLC-1 structure.

claim: Another cryoEM structure of human CLC-1 lacked density for Egate.
source: The only other CLC channel structures reported prior to 2023 are of the human CLC-1: one of these cryoEM structures shows Egate in the 'out' position (Park and MacKinnon, 2018) while the other lacked density for Egate (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited CLC-1 structure.

claim: The Egate 'out' position was originally posited to be exclusive to the CLC channel homologs.
source: The Egate 'out' position was originally posited to be exclusive to the CLC channel homologs, as its positioning off to the side widens the Cl− permeation pathway and, in CLC-1, results in a continuous pathway (Park and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: This is based on inference from the CLC-1 structure and cited work.

claim: The Egate 'out' position widens the Cl− permeation pathway.
source: The Egate 'out' position was originally posited to be exclusive to the CLC channel homologs, as its positioning off to the side widens the Cl− permeation pathway and, in CLC-1, results in a continuous pathway (Park and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of CLC-1.

claim: In CLC-1, the Egate 'out' position results in a continuous Cl− permeation pathway.
source: The Egate 'out' position was originally posited to be exclusive to the CLC channel homologs, as its positioning off to the side widens the Cl− permeation pathway and, in CLC-1, results in a continuous pathway (Park and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: This is based on the cited CLC-1 structure.

claim: A continuous Cl− permeation pathway precludes exchange coupling.
source: Such a continuous pathway precludes exchange coupling (Jardetzky, 1966; Miller, 2021).
evidence: This is based on theoretical principles of transport mechanisms cited in the literature.

claim: The open Cl− permeation pathway in the CLC-1 structure is consistent with the known functional properties of CLC-1 in the absence of an applied transmembrane voltage.
source: The open Cl− permeation pathway in the CLC-1 structure is consistent with the known functional properties of CLC-1 in the absence of an applied transmembrane (TM) voltage.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing structural and functional data.

claim: CLC-1 is a voltage-gated channel that is predominantly in the open state at zero mV.
source: CLC-1 is a voltage-gated channel that is predominantly in the open state at zero mV (Altamura et al., 2020, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: At negative TM voltages that favor CLC-1 closing, the Egate side chain presumably moves to either the 'middle' or 'down' positions, or both, to occlude the channel pore.
source: At negative TM voltages that favor CLC-1 closing, the Egate side chain presumably moves to either the 'middle' or 'down' positions, or both, to occlude the channel pore.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on known gating behavior and structural possibilities.

claim: CLC-2, like CLC-1, is a voltage-gated channel, but with opposite voltage dependence, opening instead of closing in response to hyperpolarization.
source: CLC-2, like CLC-1, is a voltage-gated channel, but with opposite voltage dependence, opening instead of closing in response to hyperpolarization (Thiemann et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: CLC-2 chloride channels are expressed in every mammalian organ.
source: CLC-2 chloride channels are expressed in every mammalian organ, where they play diverse physiological functions (Thiemann et al., 1992; Lein et al., 2007; Duan, 2013; Stölting et al., 2014; Jentsch and Pusch, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited expression and functional studies.

claim: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with human disease including leukodystrophies.
source: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with human disease including leukodystrophies (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018), blindness (Xu et al., 2023), primary aldosteronism (Fernandes-Rosa et al., 2018; Scholl et al., 2018), and atrial fibrillation (Hansen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with blindness.
source: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with human disease including leukodystrophies (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018), blindness (Xu et al., 2023), primary aldosteronism (Fernandes-Rosa et al., 2018; Scholl et al., 2018), and atrial fibrillation (Hansen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with primary aldosteronism.
source: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with human disease including leukodystrophies (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018), blindness (Xu et al., 2023), primary aldosteronism (Fernandes-Rosa et al., 2018; Scholl et al., 2018), and atrial fibrillation (Hansen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with atrial fibrillation.
source: Perturbation of CLC-2 function is associated with human disease including leukodystrophies (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018), blindness (Xu et al., 2023), primary aldosteronism (Fernandes-Rosa et al., 2018; Scholl et al., 2018), and atrial fibrillation (Hansen et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings of natively expressed CLC-2 channels reveal tremendous variation in voltage-dependent gating.
source: A mystery concerning CLC-2 is why electrophysiological recordings of natively expressed channels reveal tremendous variation in voltage-dependent gating.
evidence: This is based on observations from multiple studies in the literature.

claim: CLC-2 currents are typically inwardly rectifying and activated by hyperpolarization.
source: CLC-2 currents are typically inwardly rectifying and activated by hyperpolarization, but the kinetics and degree of rectification are highly variable (Bösl et al., 2001; Jentsch and Pusch, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: The kinetics and degree of rectification of CLC-2 currents are highly variable.
source: CLC-2 currents are typically inwardly rectifying and activated by hyperpolarization, but the kinetics and degree of rectification are highly variable (Bösl et al., 2001; Jentsch and Pusch, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: Interactions between CLC-2 and the astrocytic GlialCAM protein yield voltage-independent currents.
source: In some cases, this variability is understood – for example interactions between CLC-2 and the astrocytic GlialCAM protein yields voltage-independent currents (Jeworutzki et al., 2012; Maduke and Reimer, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: CLC-2 gating depends critically on Egate.
source: Like CLC-1, CLC-2 gating depends critically on Egate (Niemeyer et al., 2003; Cederholm et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by cited mutagenesis and functional studies.

claim: At zero mV, CLC-2 is predominantly in the closed state.
source: At zero mV, CLC-2 is predominantly in the closed state (Stölting et al., 2013; Stölting et al., 2014; Jentsch and Pusch, 2018), presumably with Egate blocking the pore.
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: At zero mV, CLC-2 presumably has Egate blocking the pore.
source: At zero mV, CLC-2 is predominantly in the closed state (Stölting et al., 2013; Stölting et al., 2014; Jentsch and Pusch, 2018), presumably with Egate blocking the pore.
evidence: This is an inference based on the closed state and known role of Egate.

claim: Egate was modeled in the pore in a recent CLC-2 cryoEM structure, but experimental density for the side chain was lacking.
source: Such pore localization for Egate was modeled in a recent CLC-2 cryoEM structure (Ma et al., 2023) however, experimental density for the side chain was lacking, and therefore the precise structure of this gate remains uncertain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This refers to a cited structure where Egate was modeled without clear density.

claim: CLC-2 gating involves interactions between Egate, Cl−, and H+, with differential effects of external vs internal ions.
source: Structures with improved resolution will be crucial to understanding CLC-2 gating, which involves interactions between Egate, Cl− , and H+, with differential effects of external vs internal ions (Pusch et al., 1999; Niemeyer et al., 2003; Sánchez-Rodríguez et al., 2010; Sánchez-Rodríguez et al., 2012; De Jesús-Pérez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: The TM region of CLC-2 displays a typical CLC family symmetric homodimeric structure.
source: The TM region of CLC-2 displays a typical CLC family symmetric homodimeric structure, with each subunit containing an independent Cl− pathway (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM structure and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Each subunit of CLC-2 contains an independent Cl− pathway.
source: The TM region of CLC-2 displays a typical CLC family symmetric homodimeric structure, with each subunit containing an independent Cl− pathway (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM structure and shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the cryoEM map, clear density for the Egate residue (E205 in CLC-2) reveals it occupying the 'down' position, at the Scen Cl−-binding site.
source: In the cryoEM map, clear density for the Egate residue (E205 in CLC-2) reveals it occupying the 'down' position, at the Scen Cl−-binding site (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The downward Egate positioning has previously been observed only in the X-ray crystallographic structure of the C. merolae CLC transporter homolog (cmCLC).
source: This downward Egate positioning has previously been observed only in the X-ray crystallographic structure of the C. merolae CLC transporter homolog (cmCLC) (Feng et al., 2010), but not in any CLC channel homolog (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to cited structures.

claim: The downward Egate positioning has not been observed in any CLC channel homolog prior to this study.
source: This downward Egate positioning has previously been observed only in the X-ray crystallographic structure of the C. merolae CLC transporter homolog (cmCLC) (Feng et al., 2010), but not in any CLC channel homolog (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This is based on comparison to all available CLC channel structures in the literature.

claim: The cryoEM map reveals a density feature at the Sext site, consistent with a bound Cl− ion.
source: Our cryoEM map also reveals a density feature at the Sext site, consistent with a bound Cl− ion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ion at the Sext site is stabilized by surrounding backbone nitrogen atoms, a characteristic feature of CLCs.
source: The ion at the Sext site is stabilized by surrounding backbone nitrogen atoms, a characteristic feature of CLCs (Dutzler et al., 2003; Picollo et al., 2009; Feng et al., 2010; Park and MacKinnon, 2018).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison to cited CLC structures.

claim: The CLC-2 structure represents a closed state, as expected at zero mV.
source: Two lines of evidence point to the structure representing a closed state, as expected at zero mV.
evidence: This is inferred from structural features and functional knowledge.

claim: Egate physically occupies the Scen Cl−-binding site, thus blocking the permeation pathway.
source: First, Egate physically occupies the Scen Cl−-binding site (Figures 1A and 2C), thus blocking the permeation pathway.
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM structure shown in Figures 1A and 2C.

claim: A continuous pathway through the CLC-2 protein could only be detected with a very small probe radius of 0.5 Å using Caver.
source: We used Caver (Chovancova et al., 2012) to detect pathways through the protein. A continuous pathway through the protein could only be detected with a very small probe radius of 0.5 Å.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of the structure using Caver software.

claim: The detected pathway in CLC-2 follows the canonical Cl− transport pathway from the extracellular side to Scen, but then circumnavigates Egate to reach the intracellular pathway.
source: In this case, the route detected follows the canonical Cl− transport pathway from the extracellular side to Scen, but then circumnavigates Egate to reach the intracellular pathway (Figure 3A, Video 1).
evidence: This is based on Caver analysis shown in Figure 3A and Video 1.

claim: The pinch point of ~0.7 Å near the Egate residue is too narrow for a Cl− ion and thus indicates a closed conformational state.
source: The pinch point of ~0.7 Å near the Egate residue is too narrow for a Cl− ion and thus indicates a closed conformational state.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and knowledge of Cl− ion size.

claim: The CLC-2 pathway is constricted compared to that in CLC-1, where the location of Egate in the 'out' position permits a wider Cl− diffusion pathway.
source: The CLC-2 pathway is constricted compared to that in CLC-1, where the location of Egate in the 'out' position permits a wider Cl− diffusion pathway (Figure 3B, Video 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the CLC-2 and CLC-1 structures shown in Figure 3B and Video 2.

claim: The location of Egate in an anion-binding site is most consistent with the side chain being negatively charged.
source: The two lines of evidence just discussed – Egate at the Scen site and the Caver pinch point – argue that Egate is in the deprotonated state: (1) the location of Egate in an anion-binding site is most consistent with the side chain being negatively charged
evidence: This is an inference based on structural and electrostatic considerations.

claim: Neutralization of Egate leads to an open-channel phenotype.
source: (2) neutralization of Egate leads to an open-channel phenotype (Niemeyer et al., 2003; de Santiago et al., 2005), which is incompatible with the observed pinched-closed pore.
evidence: This is supported by cited mutagenesis studies.

claim: The CLC-2 structure is consistent with predictions that the CLC-2 gate is formed by the Egate–TyrC pair at Scen.
source: Instead, our CLC-2 structure is consistent with the predictions made by Arreola et al., who used homology modeling in concert with detailed electrophysiological analyses to conclude that the CLC-2 gate is formed by the Egate–TyrC pair at Scen (De Jesús-Pérez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure to cited predictions.

claim: CLC-2 is the first CLC in which two conformations of the CTD are observed.
source: CLC-2 is also the first CLC in which two conformations of the CTD are observed.
evidence: This is based on comparison to all available CLC structures in the literature.

claim: Conformational change of the CTDs plays a critical role in CLC gating.
source: While many previous studies indicate that conformational change of the CTDs plays a critical role in CLC gating (Jentsch and Pusch, 2018; Grieschat et al., 2020), the mechanistic details are currently fuzzy.
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: CLC-2 can still conduct Cl− when its CTD is removed.
source: Unlike other CLC variants, CLC-2 can still conduct Cl− when its CTD is removed; however, the modified gating kinetics of this mutant do suggest a role of the CTD in regulating channel function (Garcia-Olivares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: The modified gating kinetics of CTD-deleted CLC-2 suggest a role of the CTD in regulating channel function.
source: Unlike other CLC variants, CLC-2 can still conduct Cl− when its CTD is removed; however, the modified gating kinetics of this mutant do suggest a role of the CTD in regulating channel function (Garcia-Olivares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from cited functional studies.

claim: Mutations in various regions of the CLC-2 CTD support its role in gating.
source: The impact of mutations in various regions of the CLC-2 CTD further supports its role in gating (Yusef et al., 2006; Paul et al., 2007; Stölting et al., 2013; Giorgio et al., 2017), as do the effects of ATP binding on channel kinetics (Saint-Martin et al., 2009; Stölting et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited mutagenesis and functional studies.

claim: ATP binding affects CLC-2 channel kinetics.
source: The impact of mutations in various regions of the CLC-2 CTD further supports its role in gating (Yusef et al., 2006; Paul et al., 2007; Stölting et al., 2013; Giorgio et al., 2017), as do the effects of ATP binding on channel kinetics (Saint-Martin et al., 2009; Stölting et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited functional studies.

claim: The ATP-binding site region in CLC-2 overlaps reasonably well with the structure of the ATP-bound CLC-5 CTD.
source: While we do not see ATP bound in our structure (none was added to the protein preparation), the binding site region overlaps reasonably well with the structure of the ATP-bound CLC-5 CTD (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: CTD mutations and truncations of CLC-2 occur in human leukoencephalopathy and retinal degeneration.
source: The physiological significance of an intact CTD is underscored by CTD mutations and truncations of CLC-2 that occur in human leukoencephalopathy and retinal degeneration (Giorgio et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by cited clinical and genetic studies.

claim: The structural rearrangement of the CTD strongly influences channel gating.
source: It is likely that the structural rearrangement we observe strongly influences channel gating: the CTD upward hinge rotation restricts access to the hairpin-blocking site and substantially changes CTD interactions with the TM domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed structural changes.

claim: The CTD upward hinge rotation restricts access to the hairpin-blocking site.
source: It is likely that the structural rearrangement we observe strongly influences channel gating: the CTD upward hinge rotation restricts access to the hairpin-blocking site and substantially changes CTD interactions with the TM domain.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The CTD upward hinge rotation substantially changes CTD interactions with the TM domain.
source: It is likely that the structural rearrangement we observe strongly influences channel gating: the CTD upward hinge rotation restricts access to the hairpin-blocking site and substantially changes CTD interactions with the TM domain.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The cryoEM map allowed continuous modeling of the CLC-2 sequence starting from the first TM helix (residue 88).
source: Our cryoEM map allowed continuous modeling of the CLC-2 sequence starting from the first TM helix (residue 88).
evidence: This is based on the quality of the cryoEM density map.

claim: The lack of sufficient density for modeling residues 1–87 suggests that the N terminal cytoplasmic region of CLC-2 is intrinsically disordered.
source: The lack of sufficient density for modeling residues 1–87 suggests that the N terminal cytoplasmic region of CLC-2 is intrinsically disordered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of density in the cryoEM map.

claim: The hairpin density fits perfectly with residues corresponding to 14–28.
source: We tested several candidate fragments from the CLC-2 N-terminal region and found that the hairpin density fits perfectly with residues corresponding to 14–28 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on model building into the cryoEM density shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The Q-score validation plot for residues 14-28 shows they have higher values than the Q-score expected for the corresponding resolution, indicating reliable model building.
source: Inspection of the Q-score validation plot for these residues shows they have higher values than the Q-score expected for the corresponding resolution (Figure 5B), which indicates reliable model building at this resolution (Pintilie et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on Q-score analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The best-fitting peptide from disordered regions of the C-terminal cytoplasmic region yielded poorer Q-scores than expected.
source: In contrast, the best-fitting peptide from disordered regions of the C-terminal cytoplasmic region yielded poorer Q-scores, generally lower than the Q-score expected for the corresponding resolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on Q-score analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N-terminal residues corresponding to the hairpin peptide are conserved throughout the mammalian CLC-2 homologs and partially conserved in Drosophila CLC-2.
source: The N-terminal residues corresponding to the hairpin peptide are conserved throughout the mammalian CLC-2 homologs and partially conserved in Drosophila CLC-2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The presence of the N-terminal hairpin is associated with conformational changes in the CTD and TM domains.
source: Interestingly, the presence of the N-terminal hairpin is associated with conformational changes in the CTD and TM domains.
evidence: This is observed by comparing structures with and without the hairpin.

claim: In CLC2-CTDsym, N-terminal density was observed on both subunits.
source: In CLC2-CTDsym, N-terminal density was observed on both subunits.
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map.

claim: In CLC2-CTDasym, only the subunit whose CTD adopts the 'symmetric' orientation contains the hairpin density.
source: In CLC2-CTDasym, only the subunit whose CTD adopts the 'symmetric' orientation (seen in CLC2-CTDsym) contains the hairpin density; in the subunit with the rotated CTD, no hairpin density is observed (Figure 4, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figures 4 and 5A.

claim: In the subunit with the rotated CTD, no hairpin density is observed.
source: In CLC2-CTDasym, only the subunit whose CTD adopts the 'symmetric' orientation (seen in CLC2-CTDsym) contains the hairpin density; in the subunit with the rotated CTD, no hairpin density is observed (Figure 4, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figures 4 and 5A.

claim: The subunit with the rotated CTD exhibits a difference in the linker connecting TM helices J and K, which is poorly resolved and insufficient for model building.
source: Along with the absence of hairpin density, the subunit with the rotated CTD exhibits a difference in the linker connecting TM helices J and K, which is poorly resolved and insufficient for model building.
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map.

claim: The subunits with the hairpin density contain reliable density in the JK-linker region, allowing confident modeling of an alpha helix ('JK-helix').
source: In contrast, the subunits with the hairpin density contain reliable density in the JK-linker region, allowing confident modeling of an alpha helix ('JK-helix', Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the cryoEM density map shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The JK-helix stabilizes the N-terminal hairpin peptide.
source: This observation suggests that the JK-helix stabilizes the N-terminal hairpin peptide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Residues on the JK-helix interact directly with residues at the peptide's hairpin turn.
source: Indeed, residues on the JK-helix interact directly with residues at the peptide's hairpin turn (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Interactions with other regions in the TM domain (near helices C, D, J, and R) appear to further stabilize the hairpin in its binding site.
source: Interactions with other regions in the TM domain (near helices C, D, J, and R) appear to further stabilize the hairpin in its binding site.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: The negative surface potential of the hairpin likely contributes to its interaction with the positive TM domain.
source: In addition, the negative surface potential of the hairpin likely contributes to its interaction with the positive TM domain (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Video 5).
evidence: This is based on electrostatic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and Video 5.

claim: In MD simulations, the N-terminus remained tightly associated with the channel in all simulations.
source: MD simulations help separately validate the assignment and stability of the hairpin: in MD simulations initiated from the structure, we found that the N-terminus remained tightly associated with the channel in all simulations (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on MD simulation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Delta-N CLC-2 exhibits currents that display less rectification and faster activation kinetics than WT CLC-2.
source: Delta-N CLC-2 exhibits currents that display less rectification and faster activation kinetics than WT CLC-2 (Figure 6A, B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figures 6A, B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delta-N currents are substantially larger than WT currents, ~sixfold on average when identical transfection conditions are used.
source: As was reported for N-deletion currents in oocytes, our Delta-N currents are substantially larger than WT currents, ~sixfold on average when identical transfection conditions are used (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The difference in current amplitude between WT and Delta-N cannot be explained by a difference in plasma-membrane expression.
source: This difference cannot be explained by a difference in plasma-membrane expression, as surface biotinylation experiments revealed that expression levels of the two constructs are within 30% of one another (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is based on surface biotinylation data shown in Figures 6D and E.

claim: Surface biotinylation experiments revealed that expression levels of WT and Delta-N are within 30% of one another.
source: This difference cannot be explained by a difference in plasma-membrane expression, as surface biotinylation experiments revealed that expression levels of the two constructs are within 30% of one another (Figure 6D, E).
evidence: This is based on surface biotinylation data shown in Figures 6D and E.

claim: WT but not Delta-N CLC-2 currents 'run-up' during recording sessions.
source: Strikingly, WT but not Delta-N CLC-2 currents 'run-up' during recording sessions.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F, G.

claim: The increase in WT but not Delta-N CLC-2 currents over time is consistent with an 'unblocking' of the pore by release of the N-terminal hairpin peptide.
source: The increase in WT but not Delta-N CLC-2 currents over time is consistent with an 'unblocking' of the pore by release of the N-terminal hairpin peptide.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological data and structural model.

claim: The increase in WT currents is accompanied by an apparent decrease in channel rectification, toward the level displayed by Delta-N CLC-2.
source: The increase in WT currents is accompanied by an apparent decrease in channel rectification, toward the level displayed by Delta-N CLC-2.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: AK-42 block of the augmented +80 mV currents seen at the end of each WT CLC-2 recording supports the idea that the hairpin peptide may contribute to the inward rectification of CLC-2.
source: AK-42 block of the augmented +80 mV currents seen at the end of each WT CLC-2 recording supports the idea that the hairpin peptide may contribute to the inward rectification of CLC-2 (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The structure of CLC-2 in complex with AK-42 was determined.
source: We determined the structure of CLC-2 in complex with AK-42 (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on cryoEM data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The TM domain of CLC-2 in complex with AK-42 could be resolved to 2.7 Å.
source: While the TM domain could be resolved to 2.7 Å, the CTD exhibited poor density compared to the apo sample and did not allow us to confidently model the CTD when masking the whole protein for refinement.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM data processing.

claim: The CTD in the AK-42-bound structure exhibited poor density compared to the apo sample.
source: While the TM domain could be resolved to 2.7 Å, the CTD exhibited poor density compared to the apo sample and did not allow us to confidently model the CTD when masking the whole protein for refinement.
evidence: This is based on cryoEM data quality assessment.

claim: The overall density for CLC2-TM-AK42 is very similar to that observed in apo CLC-2, but with an extra density that fits very well to the AK-42 molecule.
source: The overall density for CLC2-TM-AK42 is very similar to that observed in apo CLC-2, but with an extra density that fits very well to the AK-42 molecule (Figure 7B, Video 6).
evidence: This is based on comparison of cryoEM density maps shown in Figure 7B and Video 6.

claim: Residues in the AK-42-binding pocket exhibit little conformational change between the apo and AK-42-bound CLC-2 structures, except for residue M460.
source: Residues in the AK-42-binding pocket exhibit little conformational change between the apo and AK-42-bound CLC-2 structures. The exception is residue M460, which moves ~3 Å to avoid a clash with AK-42's phenyl ring (Figure 7—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 7.

claim: Residue M460 moves ~3 Å to avoid a clash with AK-42's phenyl ring.
source: The exception is residue M460, which moves ~3 Å to avoid a clash with AK-42's phenyl ring (Figure 7—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 7.

claim: The bound AK-42 appears to directly block Cl− permeation.
source: Located at the extracellular side of Cl− pathway, the bound AK-42 appears to directly block Cl− permeation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on the structural location of AK-42 shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The AK-42-binding pocket is the same as observed in the docking prediction previously made using a CLC-2 homology model.
source: This AK-42-binding pocket is the same as observed in the docking prediction we previously made using a CLC-2 homology model (Koster et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on comparison to cited computational docking studies.

claim: The Q-scores of AK-42 in the map are 0.74 and 0.76 in the two subunits, respectively, both higher than the expected Q-score at this resolution (0.64).
source: For the lower energy conformation, the Q-scores of AK-42 in the map are 0.74 and 0.76 in the two subunits, respectively. Both are higher than the expected Q-score at this resolution (0.64), which indicates a good fit of AK-42 to the cryoEM density (Pintilie et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on Q-score analysis of the model fit to density.

claim: A similar AK-42-binding pose was observed in another recently published structure of CLC-2.
source: A similar AK-42-binding pose was observed in another recently published structure of CLC-2 (Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on comparison to a cited structure.

claim: The RMSD between the CLC2-TM-AK42 structure and that of Ma et al. is 0.655 Å.
source: The RMSD between our CLC2-TM-AK42 structure and that of Ma et al. is 0.655 Å, and the RMSD between the apo TM structures is 0.756 Å.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: AK-42's phenyl ring nestles into a hydrophobic pocket lined by F306, F463, F459, M460, and L524.
source: In the binding site, AK-42's phenyl ring nestles into a hydrophobic pocket lined by F306, F463, F459, M460, and L524 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The carboxyl group of AK-42 forms hydrogen bonds with the side chain of S392 and backbone of K394.
source: The carboxyl group of AK-42 forms hydrogen bonds with the side chain of S392 and backbone of K394 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figure 7B.

claim: At 30 nM AK-42, inhibition of S392A is reduced ~50% compared to WT, consistent with disruption of the observed hydrogen bond.
source: These polar interactions are consistent with mutagenesis data. At 30 nM AK-42, inhibition of S392A is reduced ~50% compared to WT, consistent with disruption of the observed hydrogen bond, while inhibition of K394A is not significantly different from WT, consistent with a backbone rather than a side-chain interaction (Koster et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on cited mutagenesis data.

claim: Inhibition of K394A is not significantly different from WT, consistent with a backbone rather than a side-chain interaction.
source: These polar interactions are consistent with mutagenesis data. At 30 nM AK-42, inhibition of S392A is reduced ~50% compared to WT, consistent with disruption of the observed hydrogen bond, while inhibition of K394A is not significantly different from WT, consistent with a backbone rather than a side-chain interaction (Koster et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on cited mutagenesis data.

claim: A third hydrogen bond exists between K204 and the pyridine nitrogen of AK-42.
source: A third hydrogen bond – between K204 and the pyridine nitrogen of AK-42 – also contributes to AK-42's stability in the binding pocket.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: Inhibitor potency is increased by over two orders of magnitude by addition of a nitrogen at the pyridine position but not by addition of a nitrogen at any other position in the ring.
source: A pivotal role for the pyridine nitrogen was discovered during the development of AK-42, where it was found that inhibitor potency is increased by over two orders of magnitude by addition of a nitrogen at this position but not by addition of a nitrogen at any other position in the ring (Koster et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on cited structure-activity relationship studies.

claim: The interaction of the pyridine nitrogen with K204 is supported by mutagenesis data showing that inhibition of K204M and K204R is reduced ~threefold compared to WT.
source: The interaction of this pyridine nitrogen with K204 is supported by mutagenesis data, which shows that inhibition of K204M and K204R (K210M and K210R in rat CLC-2) is reduced ~threefold compared to WT (Koster et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on cited mutagenesis data.

claim: The distance between the nitrogen atoms on K204 and AK-42 is 3.6 Å, within acceptable hydrogen bond distance.
source: The distance between the nitrogen atoms on K204 and AK-42 is 3.6 Å, within acceptable hydrogen bond distance, while the distances between K204 and any other atoms on AK-42 are too far to allow hydrogen bond formation.
evidence: This is based on structural measurement.

claim: Density corresponding to the N-terminal hairpin structure is not seen in the AK-42-bound structure.
source: Notably, density corresponding to the N-terminal hairpin structure is not seen in the AK-42-bound structure.
evidence: This is based on examination of the cryoEM density map.

claim: The majority of AK-42-bound CLC-2 particles have a flexible N-terminus that is not blocking the Cl− pathway.
source: It thus appears that the majority of AK-42-bound CLC-2 particles have a flexible N-terminus that is not blocking the Cl− pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of hairpin density in the AK-42-bound structure.

claim: The IC50 for inhibition of CLC-2 by AK-42 (17 nM) is more than four orders of magnitude lower than the IC50 for inhibition of CLC-1.
source: The IC50 for inhibition of CLC-2 by AK-42 (17 nM) is more than four orders of magnitude lower than the IC50 for inhibition of CLC-1, CLC-2's closest homolog.
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: CLC-1 and CLC-2 are 50% identical overall.
source: CLC-1 and CLC-2 are 50% identical overall, and within the AK-42-binding site only five residues are different (Figure 7—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: Within the AK-42-binding site only five residues are different between CLC-1 and CLC-2.
source: CLC-1 and CLC-2 are 50% identical overall, and within the AK-42-binding site only five residues are different (Figure 7—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 9.

claim: The mutation S392A reduces inhibition by 30 nM AK-42 only ~threefold.
source: Indeed, the mutation S392A reduces inhibition by 30 nM AK-42 only ~threefold (Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on cited mutagenesis data.

claim: Q393P reduces inhibition by less than fivefold.
source: Similarly, Q393P (Q399P in rat CLC-2) reduces inhibition by less than fivefold (Koster et al., 2020; Ma et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on cited mutagenesis data.

claim: A steric clash between F279 in CLC-1 and the benzyl substituent in AK-42 may contribute to the lack of potency of AK-42 toward CLC-1.
source: A steric clash between F279 (F252 in CLC-2) and the benzyl substituent in AK-42 may also contribute to the lack of potency of AK-42 toward CLC-1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 9.

claim: In CLC-2, F252 is shifted away from the binding site, opening a sub-pocket that the benzyl group occupies.
source: In CLC-2, this same residue (F252) is shifted away from the binding site, opening a sub-pocket that the benzyl group occupies.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: F252 is shifted away from the binding site in the CLC-2 apo structure.
source: This difference is not simply induced by AK-42 binding, as F252 is also shifted away from the binding site in the CLC-2 apo structure.
evidence: This is based on comparison of apo and AK-42-bound structures.

claim: In structure–activity relationship studies, the benzyl substituent increased selectivity approximately fivefold.
source: In the structure–activity relationship studies used to develop AK-42, the benzyl substituent increased selectivity approximately fivefold (Koster et al., 2020), thus supporting the significance of this interaction to selectivity.
evidence: This is based on cited structure-activity relationship studies.

claim: The pathway from the extracellular solution appears sufficiently wide for AK-42 to worm its way into the binding site.
source: The pathway from the extracellular solution appears sufficiently wide for AK-42 to worm its way into the binding site (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The lack of density for the hairpin peptide in the AK-42-bound structure suggests that hairpin and AK-42 binding may be mutually exclusive.
source: Intriguingly, the lack of density for the hairpin peptide in the AK-42-bound structure suggests that hairpin and AK-42 binding may be mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: CLC-2 is the first CLC channel homolog to be seen in a closed conformational state.
source: CLC-2 is the first CLC channel homolog to be seen in a closed conformational state.
evidence: This is based on comparison to all available CLC channel structures.

claim: Egate physically occupies the Scen Cl−-binding site, thus blocking the permeation pathway in the closed state.
source: First, Egate physically occupies the Scen Cl−-binding site (Figures 1A and 2C), thus blocking the permeation pathway.
evidence: This is observed in the structure shown in Figures 1A and 2C.

claim: The pinch point of ~0.7 Å near the Egate residue indicates a closed conformational state.
source: The pinch point of ~0.7 Å near the Egate residue is too narrow for a Cl− ion and thus indicates a closed conformational state.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis using Caver.

claim: The decreased anion affinity at Scen is not the universal reason for increased Cl− conduction in CLC channels relative to the transporters.
source: However, we do not observe this occupancy, and therefore the decreased anion affinity at Scen is not the universal reason for increased Cl− conduction in CLC channels relative to the transporters.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation that Egate occupies Scen in CLC-2.

claim: The CLC-2 structure is consistent with predictions that the CLC-2 gate is formed by the Egate–TyrC pair at Scen.
source: Instead, our CLC-2 structure is consistent with the predictions made by Arreola et al., who used homology modeling in concert with detailed electrophysiological analyses to conclude that the CLC-2 gate is formed by the Egate–TyrC pair at Scen (De Jesús-Pérez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure to cited predictions.

claim: Opening of each protopore requires at least two events – relief of block by the N-terminal hairpin (ball-and-chain gating) and Egate movement.
source: At least two events are needed to open each protopore – relief of block by the N-terminal hairpin (ball-and-chain gating) and Egate movement (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the structural and functional data, illustrated in Figure 8.

claim: Ball-and-chain gating is coupled to CTD conformational change: rotation of the CTD toward the membrane precludes hairpin binding, thus facilitating channel opening.
source: A key aspect of our revised framework is that ball-and-chain gating is coupled to CTD conformational change: close examination of the state with the CTD rotated (Figure 4A) reveals that the hairpin cannot access its pore-blocking site in this state. Thus, CTD rotation facilitates hairpin release and channel opening.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The hairpin cannot access its pore-blocking site when the CTD is rotated.
source: A key aspect of our revised framework is that ball-and-chain gating is coupled to CTD conformational change: close examination of the state with the CTD rotated (Figure 4A) reveals that the hairpin cannot access its pore-blocking site in this state.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CTD rotation facilitates hairpin release and channel opening.
source: Thus, CTD rotation facilitates hairpin release and channel opening.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Removal of the CTD speeds CLC-2 activation and deactivation kinetics.
source: This structural model is consistent with electrophysiological studies showing that removal of the CTD speeds CLC-2 activation and deactivation kinetics (Garcia-Olivares et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: In CLC-2, the CTDs can move independently of one another.
source: In contrast to CLC-0, where movements in the CTD have been linked to the highly cooperative conformational change involved in common gating (Estévez et al., 2004; Bykova et al., 2006), our structures illustrate that in CLC-2 the CTDs can move independently of one another.
evidence: This is based on the observation of asymmetric CTD conformations in the structure.

claim: Even when Egate is neutralized, CLC-2 retains some voltage-dependent gating.
source: Even when Egate is neutralized, CLC-2 retains some voltage-dependent gating (Niemeyer et al., 2003), indicating a conformational change beyond Egate.
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: Channels with N-terminal deletions retain biexponential voltage dependence as is seen in the wild-type channels.
source: This additional voltage-dependent gating cannot be solely due to N-terminal ball-and-chain gating, since channels with N-terminal deletions retain biexponential voltage dependence as is seen in the wild-type channels (Varela et al., 2002).
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: Electrophysiological studies indicate that CLC-2 has at least two open states.
source: Second, electrophysiological studies indicate that CLC-2 has at least two open states (de Santiago et al., 2005), but the physical basis for these different open states is unknown.
evidence: This is based on cited functional studies.

claim: Channel rectification changes upon N-terminal deletion or ball-and-chain gating.
source: Augmenting complexity in understanding CLC-2 is our observation that channel rectification changes upon N-terminal deletion or ball-and-chain gating (Figure 6F; Figure 6—figure supplement 2): the molecular underpinnings of this change in rectification are wholly unknown.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.
